source: Ge, Zhang & Vorobeychik (2026) Mind the (DH) Gap! A Contrast in Risky Choices Between Reasoning and Conversational LLMs (ACL 2026)
finding: 20 frontier and open LLMs split into two behaviour clusters on risky choice: reasoning models (RMs) and conversational models (CMs). RMs are close to a risk-neutral expected-payoff maximiser. CMs are not. Neither group is close to humans. Gap 4: yes, reasoning models are close to EV maximisers.
numbers: Within-cluster pairwise correlation of choice rates above 0.8, mostly 0.9 or higher; across clusters 0.6 or below. RM vs expected-payoff agent correlation 0.86 to 1; CM vs expected-payoff agent below 0.5. Best LLM-human correlation only 0.42 (Claude-4.5-Haiku, a CM); RMs further from humans than CMs. Human vs expected-payoff agent correlation 0.14 (prospects were picked to emphasise human deviations). 360 Prolific participants; each LLM condition queried 10 times at temperature 1; 50 samples changed little. Paired open models: Qwen2.5-Instruct is a CM, its math-reasoning variant an RM; same for Qwen3-30B and Olmo-3-7B; authors say math-reasoning fine-tuning is the key differentiator.
quote: RMs are insensitive to the order of prospects, gain/loss framing, and explanations
limits: Prospect set is small and chosen to stress human deviations. Not a test of whether EV-maximising is better for real decisions. Only choice rates, no human-value stakes. Opened via PDF text (v2, 20 Apr 2026).
agent_relevance: If our agent uses a reasoning-mode model, its lottery-style choices will be near expected value and insensitive to order and framing. That is useful for numeric choices and is a different thing from human-like value trade-offs.

source: Ge, Zhang & Vorobeychik (2026) Mind the (DH) Gap! A Contrast in Risky Choices Between Reasoning and Conversational LLMs (ACL 2026)
finding: Description-history (DH) gap: when a gamble is shown as a list of sampled past outcomes instead of explicit odds, every LLM moves toward humans and away from the expected-payoff agent. The shift is small for frontier reasoning models and large for conversational models. Gap 7: the gap is a bigger lever than loss aversion for chat models and mostly absent for frontier reasoning models.
numbers: For all frontier models, explicit to implicit presentation raises similarity to humans and lowers similarity to the expected-payoff agent. GPT-5.1 and DeepSeek-R1 barely change. CMs change dramatically and cluster closely under implicit prospects. Open RMs (7B to 32B) do show a large gap, sharper for 30B/32B than 7B. Humans become more EV-like under implicit prospects. Several LLMs are more rational with 100-sample histories than with 20-sample histories, so context length is not the cause (128K contexts).
limits: The paper reports the gap mainly as 2D similarity plots (Figs 4, 5), not one decisiveness number per model. I could not get a single headline decisiveness figure from the text; per-model numbers sit in figures and appendix tables.
agent_relevance: Our agent should not assume that a task given as logged past outcomes behaves like a task given as stated odds. If the scaffold feeds the agent tool-run histories, test both forms.

source: Ge, Zhang & Vorobeychik (2026) Mind the (DH) Gap! A Contrast in Risky Choices Between Reasoning and Conversational LLMs (ACL 2026)
finding: Order, framing and explanation sensitivity differ by cluster. CMs are strongly order-sensitive and frame-sensitive. Asking for a longer rationale often lowers rationality in CMs. Humans are less frame-sensitive than CMs.
numbers: Decisiveness (mean of max(p,1-p)) is high for all LLMs, higher than for the human pool; RMs more decisive than CMs. Consistency to order, prompt (explanation type: none, one-sentence, math rationale) and frame (gain vs loss): RMs near fully invariant, CMs not. Long rationale lowers EV-likeness in frontier and open CMs; Claude-4.5-Haiku is an exception (both explanation types made it less EV-like than none).
limits: Numbers are in a heatmap (Fig 3); I did not extract cell values. The appendix prompt-sensitivity check (three wordings) supports that the RM-CM gap holds.
agent_relevance: Frame invariance is cheap for reasoning models and costly for chat models. Asking a chat model for a long rationale is not a safe debiasing step.

source: Kraishan (2026) The Long Road to the Same Answer: Cognitive Bias Under Escalating Reasoning Budgets in LLMs
finding: Dose-response test: does more thinking shrink cognitive bias? Not reliably. Reasoning models were not less biased than matched non-reasoning siblings; the point estimate leaned the other way in every family. No slope of bias against realised reasoning tokens was significantly negative.
numbers: 30 vignettes (6 biases x 5 items: anchoring, framing, loss aversion, escalation of commitment, availability, confirmation), 7 models from 4 families (Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepSeek, Qwen), requested thinking ceilings 0, 1,024, 4,096, 8,192 tokens, 12,350 API calls. Reasoning minus sibling bias magnitude: Delta +0.031, 95% bootstrap CI [-0.010, +0.074], t(29)=1.45, p=.157, dz=0.27. Realised tokens differed from the ceiling: GPT-5.1 used about 116 to 118 tokens whatever the ceiling; DeepSeek-R1 used 1,074 to 1,617 on average even at budget 0, and 79% of R1 calls exceeded the 1,024 ceiling.
limits: Five items per bias, so item-level tests have low power. Vignette benchmark, not lottery fitting. Single preprint, one author. Bias score is a signed shift against a control prompt.
agent_relevance: At equal or larger token budgets, extra thinking alone does not remove bias. A bias-specific step has to be in the scaffold. Supports explicit checks over just 'think longer'.

source: Kraishan (2026) The Long Road to the Same Answer: Cognitive Bias Under Escalating Reasoning Budgets in LLMs
finding: Per-bias results: only anchoring goes in the human direction. Framing is reliably reversed. Loss aversion is directional but not significant. A one-line debiasing instruction (restate the anchor) lowered anchoring on all five items where extra thinking did not.
numbers: Anchoring d=1.89 (human direction). Framing mean signed score -0.336, 95% CI [-0.403,-0.245], t(4)=-7.57, pHolm=.010, d=-2.35 (reversed). Loss aversion M=-0.586, 95% CI [-0.914,+0.031], t(4)=-1.91, pHolm=.256, d=-0.88 (directional, reversed vs humans). Four of the other five biases lean opposite to humans in all seven models. Anchor restatement lowered anchoring on 5 of 5 items, p=.057. Authors note the loss-aversion reversal looks like what a risk-neutral EV maximiser would give.
quote: A one-line instruction to restate the anchor before answering lowered anchoring
limits: n=5 items per bias; Holm correction; one instruction tested; no accuracy on real tasks.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 partly: a targeted one-line step beat added thinking tokens on anchoring. For loss aversion and framing, models already lean away from the human bias, so a debias step may over-correct.

source: Lyu, Ren, Feng, Wang, Chen, Ren & de Rijke (2025) Self-Adaptive Cognitive Debiasing for LLMs in Decision-Making (SACD)
finding: A scaffold step that detects bias in the prompt, analyses it and rewrites the prompt (up to 3 rounds) cut measured bias scores much more than few-shot, CoT, Reflexion, multi-agent debate or one-pass self-help debiasing. Gap 1: yes on bias scores, at the cost of extra calls.
numbers: Bias score = share choosing the biased target in treatment minus control, range -1 to 1. Average bias score vanilla -> SACD: FOMC llama3.1-8b 0.3805 -> 0.1570; PubMedQA 8b 0.4425 -> 0.1790; PubMedQA 70b 0.4730 -> 0.0560; LegalBench 8b 0.5570 -> 0.1235. Loss-aversion column: FOMC 8b vanilla 0.2100, SACD 0.1560, self-help 0.2860 (worse than vanilla); PubMedQA 8b 0.2340 -> 0.1860. 500 samples per setting for llama 8b/70b and gpt-3.5-turbo, 100 for gpt-4o, temperature 0, max 3 iterations.
limits: 'Loss aversion bias' here is a prompt that warns of severe punishment for a wrong decision; it is not lottery lambda. Bias score measures drift from control, not task accuracy; I found no equal-token accuracy table in the paper text. Cost is several LLM calls per item (3 steps per iteration, up to 3 iterations). Models are llama3.1, gpt-3.5-turbo, gpt-4o; no reasoning models.
agent_relevance: A detect-analyse-rewrite step is a candidate operator for prompts that carry pressure cues (threat of blame, stakes). Needs its own equal-token and real-accuracy test in our harness.

source: Lyu, Ren, Feng, Wang, Chen, Ren & de Rijke (2025) Self-Adaptive Cognitive Debiasing for LLMs in Decision-Making (SACD)
finding: Some popular steps backfire. CoT and few-shot raised bias scores in some cells, and multi-bias prompts hit baselines hardest.
numbers: PubMedQA llama3.1-70b loss-aversion score: vanilla 0.3100, CoT 0.9440, few-shot 0.2920, Reflexion 0.4440, multi-agent debate 0.5380, self-help 0.0340, SACD 0.0320. PubMedQA llama3.1-8b few-shot average 0.8105 vs vanilla 0.4425. FOMC 8b multi-agent debate average 0.5020 vs vanilla 0.3805. Error analysis: self-help debiasing had 257 insufficient-debiasing errors (51.4%) vs 61 (12.2%) for SACD in one comparison.
limits: Single-run cells at temperature 0; no confidence intervals in the tables I read. Large swings suggest prompt-specific effects.
agent_relevance: Do not add CoT or debate as a default debias step; measure each per bias.

source: Lim, Kim & Whang (2026) DeFrame: Debiasing LLMs Against Framing Effects
finding: Re-framing step: a 4-call prompt that restates the question in alternative framings, writes guidelines and self-revises cuts framing-induced disparity. This is fairness framing (e.g. 'A is better than B' vs 'B is worse than A'), not Tversky-Kahneman gain/loss framing, so it transfers only by analogy.
numbers: 8 instruct LLMs; on BBQ DeFrame reduced framing disparity by 92% and bias score by 93% on average. In BBQ, bias under negative framings was on average 2x larger than under positive framings, up to 4x. Baselines (debiasing prompt, self-revision, IF-CoT, 1 to 2 calls) lowered average bias but often left disparity or made it worse; on 70Decisions-Framed their effects were unstable. Ablation: more stages gave more stability at higher inference cost.
limits: Fairness benchmarks (BBQ, DoNotAnswer-Framed, 70Decisions-Framed), not lotteries or accuracy. Inference cost is 4 calls per question versus 1 for plain, so it is not an equal-token comparison.
agent_relevance: Supports an operator that re-states a problem in a second framing and checks the answer is the same. Cost is about 4x calls.

source: Yechiam & Tarabeih (2026) Mimicry Without Understanding: The Origins of Decision Bias in LLMs
finding: Gap 3 partly: telling a model about human behaviour in the prompt moves its loss aversion. When the prompt said humans were loss averse, lambda rose; when it said humans seek gains, lambda fell. Tested only in ChatGPT-4o and Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, no reasoning models.
numbers: Study 3, prompted human behaviour: ChatGPT lambda 1.257 (large sample) / 1.218 (small) in the loss-aversion condition vs 1.072 in gain-seeking; Qwen 1.742 for both vs 0.940 / 0.929. 100 agents per cell. Effect was largest at the indifference point (-$5/+$6) for ChatGPT, B=1.46, SE=0.34, p<.001.
limits: The prompt reported behaviour of other humans, not a bias name in a system prompt. Two models, one lab group (same group as Tarabeih 2026, so not independent of K07-K11). Preprint.
agent_relevance: Any scaffold text that says 'people usually avoid losses' may inject that bias. Keep bias descriptions out of the agent's working prompt unless a debias step is the purpose.

source: Yechiam & Tarabeih (2026) Mimicry Without Understanding: The Origins of Decision Bias in LLMs
finding: Real scientific abstracts and full papers on loss aversion shifted LLM lambda in the direction of the paper's own finding, a self-fulfilling-prophecy effect. The paper with the strongest reported human loss aversion produced the strongest LLM loss aversion.
numbers: Study 4a, 800 sessions (100 per condition x 2 models x 4 conditions incl. no-paper control). ChatGPT lambda 1.785 after the Brown et al. abstract (strong human loss aversion) vs 1.043 after the Yechiam & Zeif abstract (no loss aversion); Qwen 1.170 vs 1.047. ChatGPT control 1.09. ChatGPT accepted 105% more lotteries given Yechiam & Zeif than Brown; Qwen 9% more. Regression chi2(7)=1,043, McFadden r2=0.58. Study 4b full report: ChatGPT 1.52 after Brown. Qwen could not take full papers due to length.
limits: Gap 3 for reasoning models stays open: none were tested. Fixed lottery design (loss $5 to $10 vs gain $6); one author group.
agent_relevance: Bias knowledge placed in context can raise the bias; use bias descriptions only in a separate check step and measure before and after.

source: Brown, Imai, Vieider & Camerer (2021 working paper; 2024 J Econ Lit 62(2):485-516) Meta-analysis of empirical estimates of loss aversion
finding: Gap 2: the largest human meta-analysis puts mean lambda near 1.96, below 2.25, and the raw median at 1.69.
numbers: 607 estimates from 150 articles. Bayesian random-effects mean 1.955, 95% CrI [1.824, 2.104]. Raw median 1.69 (n=522). By type: aggregate-level 286 estimates, mean 1.955, SD 1.667, median 1.545; individual-level medians 162, mean 1.829, SD 0.759; individual-level means 159, higher and skewed. Among 85 studies with both, mean of means 3.47 (median 2.08), mean of medians 1.71. Tversky-Kahneman 1992 original: 25 students, median 2.25, unincentivised.
limits: Estimates come from many designs; 1.955 is pooled across designs, not a design-matched target. Large heterogeneity (14.4% of between-observation variance explained by covariates). I read the 2021 working paper; the published version may differ slightly.
agent_relevance: Use 1.7 to 2.0 only as a general human reference; do not hard-code 2.25.

source: Brown et al. (2021/2024) meta-regression and publication bias section
finding: Moderators of human lambda: field experiments and general-population samples give higher values than lab and student samples; survey tasks give lower values than binary lottery choice; money vs non-money reward made no clear difference; value-function form and reference point mattered little. Funnel plots showed asymmetry for aggregate estimates and individual-level means, much less for medians.
numbers: Baseline: individual mean, lab, university population, hypothetical money, binary choice, K-T definition. 14.4% of between-observation variance explained. The Kobberling-Wakker definition gave modestly higher lambda than the K-T definition.
limits: Moderator effects read from prose and a forest plot, not the coefficient table (Table C.1 online appendix). Funnel asymmetry is partly a measurement-type artefact per the authors.
agent_relevance: A design-matched human target needs: lottery choice task, symmetric ranges, one reward type. No dataset gives that single number yet. Gap 2 stays partly open.

source: Yechiam & Zeif (2025) Loss aversion is not robust: A re-meta-analysis (J Econ Psychol 107)
finding: Re-analysis of the Brown et al. dataset: strong loss aversion held when losses were smaller than gains and when items were presented in an ordered way, but for symmetric, unordered lotteries lambda was about 1.07, not significantly above 1.
numbers: 84 papers, 163 estimates, n=149,218 participants. Symmetric unordered lotteries lambda approximately 1.07 (not significantly above 1.0).
limits: Read from the abstract on the IDEAS page, not the full paper. Inclusion rules differ from Brown et al.; critique.md already notes the two disagree because of selection. No peer rebuttal found this session.
agent_relevance: For an agent tested on symmetric lotteries, the best human reference is about 1.07, so an agent near 1.0 is not 'too rational'. For loss-skewed designs the reference is 1.8 to 2.0.

source: Wang, Lin, Liu et al. (2025, v5 Sep 2026) Rethinking Prospect Theory for LLMs: Revealing the Instability of Decision-Making under Epistemic Uncertainty
finding: Gaps 5 and 6: prospect theory does not describe all LLMs well. Fit quality and lambda vary by model, and small models fit poorly.
numbers: Baseline PT parameters (risk preference, lambda, probability weighting, MAE, McFadden R2): Human (Tanaka 2010) 0.670, 2.630, 0.685. Llama-3.1-8B 0.585, 0.010, 0.753, MAE 0.332, R2 0.092. Mistral-7B 0.534, 0.570, 0.577, 0.155, 0.132. Qwen2.5-7B 0.429, 0.010, 3.645, 0.047, 0.116. Qwen2.5-14B 0.503, 1.909, 0.896, 0.257, 0.067. Qwen2.5-32B 0.598, 1.213, 0.867, 0.161, 0.225. GPT-5-Mini 0.447, 4.000, 2.888, 0.115, 0.206. Gemini-2.5-Flash 0.495, 1.499, 0.814, 0.134, 0.225. Authors treat MAE above 0.20 as unreliable and pseudo-R2 below 0.10 as poor. 256 samples per lottery, temperature 0.7.
limits: Column meaning read from the extracted table layout (first risk preference, then lambda, then weighting). Several lambdas sit at the bounds (0.010, 4.000), which signals non-identifiable fits. Does not test the 1979 problems P1-P14.
agent_relevance: Do not report lambda for an agent without fit quality and sampling settings. Bound-hitting values mean 'no stable lambda'.

source: Wang, Lin, Liu et al. (2025, v5 Sep 2026) Rethinking Prospect Theory for LLMs: Revealing the Instability of Decision-Making under Epistemic Uncertainty (epistemic-marker stage)
finding: Replacing numeric probabilities with words like 'unlikely' moves loss aversion and probability weighting a lot, risk preference only mildly. Bigger models are steadier but not stable.
numbers: Marker-to-probability mappings kept a consistent rank order across models. Under matched mean probabilities, loss aversion and weighting shifted more than risk preference; some small-model estimates hit parameter bounds. Qwen2.5-32B was comparatively stable yet still varied across conditions. Its baseline lambda here is 1.213, against the 0.95 to 2.01 spread across rounds noted earlier (a27/c03).
limits: No matched human baseline for the marker stage (authors say so). Temperature 0.7 only. The paper gives no rule for how many runs give a trustworthy lambda; it used 256 samples per lottery.
agent_relevance: Verbal-uncertainty text in agent prompts can change risk behaviour. For a stable lambda, use a few hundred samples per lottery and report the spread across wordings.

source: Replicating patterns of prospect theory for territorial decision under risk (OSF/PsyArXiv preprint v2, 2025)
finding: Gap 8: two preregistered replications of Ruggeri et al. (2020) with territorial dilemmas instead of money. Most items replicated. The reflection effect was not robust. The record shows a preprint with no journal DOI or peer-review detail.
numbers: US N=149, UK N=253. Item-level replication 69% (Study 1) and 81% (Study 2). Theoretical contrasts (five prospect theory patterns) 77% (Study 1) and 92% (Study 2). Certainty, framing, isolation and small-probability overweighting held. Posted to PsyArXiv 28 Jul 2025, modified 21 Aug 2025; review state 'accepted' on the preprint server only.
limits: Preprint-server 'accepted' is not journal peer review. Boundary condition: territorial, not monetary, outcomes. Reflection is the weak pattern.
agent_relevance: Gain/loss reflection is the least portable pattern. If our agent is tested on reflection items, expect lower human agreement than for certainty and framing.

source: Dubedy (2026) Persona-Conditioned Risk Behavior in LLMs: A Simulated Gambling Study with GPT-4.1
finding: Gap 9: personas strongly change risk behaviour inside a gambling task, but the paper does not test leakage into neutral tasks. The persona text also carried a different goal instruction, so persona and goal are confounded.
numbers: 3 personas: Rich $10,000 ('Preserve wealth and avoid unnecessary risk'), Middle $500 ('steady growth while managing risk'), Poor $50 ('Take calculated risks to improve your financial situation'). 50 iterations per condition, 6,950 decisions, GPT-4.1, temperature 1.0. Rounds played: Poor 37.4 (SD 15.5) vs Rich 1.1 (SD 0.31); Kruskal-Wallis H=393.5. Risk score means: Rich 17.53, Middle 40.23, Poor 63.36; d=4.15 Poor vs Rich, 1.85 Middle vs Rich, 2.89 Poor vs Middle. A fourth Explorer persona was blocked by content moderation.
limits: One independent researcher, one model, no human data, no neutral-task transfer test, no guardrail tested. Goal text differs by persona, so d=4.15 cannot be put down to wealth alone.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 stays open. A guardrail idea: strip wealth and role cues from prompts for tasks where they are not needed, then test with a neutral decision.

source: Ethayarajh, Xu, Muennighoff, Jurafsky & Kiela (2024) KTO: Model Alignment as Prospect Theoretic Optimization (loss-weight section)
finding: Gap 10: loss weights lambda_D and lambda_U are training-time hyperparameters in KTO. The paper gives no scaffold-side (inference-time) use of loss weighting.
numbers: Default lambda_D = lambda_U = 1. Rule: 1 <= lambda_D*n_D / (lambda_U*n_U) <= 3/2. With a 1:10 desirable:undesirable ratio, set lambda_U=1 and lambda_D in [10,15]; dropping 90% of desirable data used lambda_D=13.33 and KTO still beat DPO. Gain sensitivity gave better results than loss sensitivity on most benchmarks; toxicity prevention is named as a case where more loss weight may help. A risk-neutral (identity) value function collapsed BBH performance. Memory-light variant without a reference model: lambda_D=1.75 beat DPO on some tasks; 1.5 or 2.0 lowered GSM8K and BBH by several points.
limits: Training loss only. It uses the CPT shape (reference point, concavity, loss aversion) to weight examples, not to model the agent's own choices.
agent_relevance: No direct scaffold use found. An analogue would be weighting false-positive and false-negative costs in a check step; that is a design choice, not a result from this paper.
